title: AI and the worker: BMS calls for global regulation
author: Editorial Desk
summary: At an international congress in April 2025, BMS asked governments to put guardrails around artificial intelligence.
body:
*Photo: BMS at an international congress on AI and work, April 2025*

In April 2025, the Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh told an international congress in Turkey that governments should set up **regulatory mechanisms for artificial intelligence (AI)**, so that workers are protected from job loss and the gains of higher productivity are shared. This post explains where and how the message was delivered, what the BMS position is, what international evidence says about AI and jobs, and why unions need to engage early.

## The setting: Ankara, 18 to 21 April 2025

According to a BMS press statement published on 22 April 2025, the **International Congress on Labour Digitalization and Social Justice** was held in Ankara from 18 to 21 April 2025. It was organised by Memur-Sen, a Turkish central trade union. More than 200 delegates from 36 countries attended. Turkey's Deputy Foreign Minister opened it, the Labour Minister addressed it on the second day, and Memur-Sen's president presided. The congress had four plenary sessions and four panels, and it closed by adopting a seven-point Ankara Declaration on Labour, Digitalization and Social Justice.

India was represented by a six-member delegation drawn from three central trade union organisations: BMS, the Trade Union Coordination Centre and the National Federation of Independent Trade Unions. The BMS delegation was led by General Secretary Ravindra Himte, who spoke on protecting labour interests in the digital era. BMS All India Organising Secretary Surendran Bojji moderated one of the panels. The delegation also met India's Ambassador to Turkey at the Indian Embassy in Ankara to discuss Indian migrant workers in several countries.

## The two sides of AI

AI can raise productivity, take over dangerous or repetitive tasks and create new kinds of work. It can also replace jobs, intensify surveillance and put decisions about hiring, pay and discipline in the hands of algorithms that no worker can question. A warehouse worker whose pace is set by a software score, a driver rated by an app, a clerk whose tasks are automated: each of these illustrates how the technology reaches the workplace.

The International Labour Organization and Poland's National Research Institute released a study on 20 May 2025, shortly after the congress, on exposure to generative AI. It found that about 25 per cent of global employment is in occupations potentially exposed, rising to 34 per cent in high-income countries. Clerical jobs face the highest exposure, and women face higher exposure: in high-income countries 9.6 per cent of female employment is in the jobs at the highest level of exposure, against 3.5 per cent for men. The authors stress that these are measures of potential exposure and not of actual job losses, and that transformation of jobs is more likely than outright replacement. They also call on governments, employers' organisations and workers' organisations to engage in social dialogue and build proactive, inclusive strategies.

## The BMS position

As reported on the BMS website, the organisation's message at Ankara was that:

- governments should **regulate AI** by setting up regulatory mechanisms, and the delegation called for rules covering AI, machine learning and the Internet of Things;
- workers should be protected against **job displacement**, with productivity improvements used for their benefit;
- the benefits of technology are real, but it can have what BMS called an "impersonal and inhuman impact";
- productivity gains should reach **workers** as well as owners;
- technology should be a **tool of human development**, not a replacement for human beings.

The BMS statement describes the main demand as global regulation of AI and digital technology to protect workers. It does not list a detailed legal proposal, and the position is best read as a call to begin the work of regulation, with workers at the table.

## The bigger frame

This sits well with the BMS motto *Rashtra hit, Udyog hit, Mazdoor hit*, meaning the interest of the nation, of industry and of the worker. Technology is welcome when it serves all three. A technology that raises output but pushes a million families into insecurity does not meet that test. The same logic runs through BMS positions on wages, social security and safety: growth is judged by what it does for the person doing the work.

## Why unions must engage

Trade unions that wait until a technology is deployed find that the decisions have already been taken. Engaging early is the practical way to shape how AI enters the workplace. Possible routes include:

- **Consultation.** Workers should be informed and consulted before an AI system is introduced for hiring, scheduling, monitoring or discipline.
- **Collective bargaining.** Agreements can cover retraining, redeployment, notice periods and transparency about how automated tools are used.
- **Law.** Governments can set minimum standards on transparency, the right to human review of automated decisions, and data protection at work.
- **Skills.** Re-skilling should be a right and not a favour, with time and money provided by employers and the State.

The ILO study noted that digital transition policies will be a major factor in whether workers are retained and how job quality is affected. That is another way of saying that the outcome is not fixed by the technology. It depends on choices made by governments, employers and workers' organisations.

## International solidarity

BMS also used the Ankara meeting to build links. Three Indian central trade union organisations sent delegates, and the panels covered globalisation and digitalisation, social justice and income distribution, organisational diversity and global solidarity, and digitalisation's impact on trade union structures. Many of the questions AI raises, such as platform work across borders or data collected in one country and used in another, cannot be solved by one country alone, which is why the call for international cooperation on rules matters.

## What remains to be done

The call for regulation is the beginning. A number of things have to follow: a national discussion in India among Government, employers and unions on how AI should be governed at work; protection for the workers who are most exposed, such as clerical staff and women in routine jobs; training pathways for those whose tasks change; and monitoring of how algorithms are used in recruitment and management. Unions themselves need to build expertise, so that they can ask the right questions of a vendor or an employer.

## Closing

AI will not wait for a perfect law. What BMS has asked is that governments take responsibility early, that workers have a voice, and that gains from technology are shared. That is a modest and practical demand.
